entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Bukki, a pivotal figure in the post-Mosaic Israelite priesthood, served as the fifth High Priest of the Israelites, a lineage tracing directly to Aaron, the brother of Moses. His tenure, though not explicitly dated, is traditionally placed during the tumultuous period of the Judges, approximately 12th-11th centuries BCE, an era preceding the Israelite monarchy. His significance lies in maintaining the sacerdotal continuity and the sanctity of the Levitical succession, thereby ensuring the unbroken transmission of religious authority and ritual practice crucial to the nascent Israelite religious identity. He solidified the institutional framework of the Tabernacle worship during a period of political decentralization and moral ambiguity.

As the son of Abishua and father of Uzzi, Bukki inherited the high priestly office, a sacred responsibility detailed in the biblical genealogies found in the Book of Chronicles (1 Chronicles 6:4–5) and Ezra (Ezra 7:4). The High Priest's duties included officiating on the Day of Atonement, consulting the Urim and Thummim for divine guidance, and guiding the spiritual life of the twelve tribes. While specific events of Bukki's personal high priesthood are not enumerated in the biblical texts, his very existence in the lineage ensured the continuity of the Aaronic covenant and the Mosaic Law's implementation during a fragmented period when 'everyone did what was right in his own eyes' (Judges 17:6). He presided over the ceremonial rituals that reinforced national identity and adherence to Yahweh.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Bukki's significance stems from his role in maintaining the unbroken lineage of the Israelite High Priesthood during a crucial formative period, ensuring the continuity of religious authority and ritual practice. His position helped solidify the institutional framework of early Israelite religion, influencing subsequent Jewish religious identity.
